solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Team’s requirement for maximum break (3,6)

blocks.note: New Zealand's rugby union side, named for its black strip
a snooker maximum of 147 needs the black potted after every red

annotation.surface: A captain listing what the side needs to win a snooker match.
annotation.walkthrough: In snooker a break is a run of pots, and the 147 maximum is only reachable by taking the black, the highest-scoring colour, after each of the fifteen reds. The 's stands for 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: The All Blacks are the national rugby side of New Zealand, named for their black strip.

entries.clue: Strolled in the morning, then ran (6)

annotation.surface: Someone takes a gentle morning walk and then breaks into a run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ran' looks like the opposite of strolling, but it is the dye sense: colours in the wash ran, or bled.
annotation.definitionFit: To amble is to walk at a slow, relaxed pace, so strolled is ambled.

entries.clue: Weapon that may be put before corporal (5)

annotation.definition2: that may be put before corporal

blocks.note: a long spear carried by a horseman

blocks.clueFragment: that may be put before corporal
blocks.note: the word in front of corporal names the lowest non-commissioned rank in the British Army

annotation.surface: A soldier's weapon being presented to the corporal on parade.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half is a fill-in-the-blank: the word that goes in front of corporal to make a rank.
annotation.definitionFit: A lance is a long thrusting weapon used by mounted soldiers.

entries.clue: Sit at ease with one fizzy drink and sweet (8)

blocks.note: to loll is to lounge lazily
pop is a fizzy soft drink

annotation.surface: Lounging about with a fizzy drink and something sugary: a lazy afternoon.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' simply strings the pieces together; the sweet at the end is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by example: a lollipop is one kind of sweet, a boiled sweet on a stick.

entries.clue: New cartoonist mixed up lake (8,5)

annotation.surface: A newly hired cartoonist who is confused about something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New' looks like an anagram signal but is part of the fodder; 'mixed up' is the indicator. Coniston Water is a lake in the English Lake District.
annotation.definitionFit: Coniston Water is a lake in Cumbria, famous for Donald Campbell's speed records.

entries.clue: All four directions linked together (4)

annotation.surface: The four points of the compass joined up in one statement.
annotation.walkthrough: The compass points can be taken in any order; only this order spells a word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: stitching joins pieces of cloth, so sewn things are linked together.

entries.clue: Fiction book provided must be returned (3)

indicatorNotes.must be returned: something returned goes back the way it came

annotation.surface: A library rule: a borrowed novel has to be brought back.
annotation.walkthrough: The library surface makes 'returned' look like handing a book in; here it sends B + IF backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A fib is a small lie, and a lie is a fiction.

entries.clue: Violently refute a prominent story (7)

indicatorNotes.Violently: the letters are thrown about violently

annotation.surface: Someone angrily denying a front-page newspaper story.
annotation.walkthrough: The newspaper setting makes 'story' feel like the thing being refuted, but the refuting word is the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A feature is a prominent article in a newspaper or magazine.

entries.clue: Cheers a couple of runs (3-3)

blocks.note: cheers is a casual British goodbye
a bye in cricket is a run scored when the ball passes the batsman untouched

annotation.surface: Applause for a batsman who has scored two runs.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain 'cheers' is also a way of saying goodbye. In cricket a bye is a run taken off a ball that nobody hits, so two of them are BYE BYE.
annotation.definitionFit: Bye-bye is an informal farewell, just as cheers is.

entries.clue: To exclude a learner is commonplace (5)

blocks.note: L = learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

annotation.surface: Turning away a student is an everyday occurrence.
annotation.walkthrough: The L comes from the L-plates that learner drivers in Britain must display.
annotation.definitionFit: Something banal is ordinary and unoriginal, that is commonplace.

entries.clue: Old prison replaced entrance (7)

annotation.surface: An old jail whose main doorway has been renewed.
annotation.walkthrough: Newgate was London's notorious prison, demolished in 1904; the Old Bailey stands on its site.
annotation.definitionFit: Newgate was a prison in the City of London for over seven centuries.

entries.clue: Stage I placed in a certain direction for lamenting poet (8)

indicatorNotes.placed in: the first pieces are put inside the direction

blocks.note: a leg is a stage of a journey or race
one of the compass directions; LEGI goes inside it

annotation.surface: A theatre direction: put me on stage facing one way to play a mournful poet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stage' looks theatrical, but it is a leg of a journey. 'A certain direction' is vague on purpose: only EAST will take LEGI and make a word.
annotation.definitionFit: An elegiast writes elegies, poems of lament for the dead.

entries.clue: Purchase retains nothing in float (4)

indicatorNotes.retains: the outer word keeps the inner letter held within it

annotation.surface: A shopper spends nothing on a float, perhaps for a parade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Float' is a noun here: a buoy is a floating marker.
annotation.definitionFit: A buoy is an anchored float marking a channel or hazard.

entries.clue: Conspicuously recruit colleague (8)

blocks.note: to sign a player is to recruit them
an ally is a colleague or partner

annotation.surface: A manager very visibly bringing a new team-mate on board.
annotation.walkthrough: SIGNALLY is an uncommon adverb, meaning strikingly; think of 'signally failed'.
annotation.definitionFit: Signally means notably or conspicuously, as in 'signally failed'.

entries.clue: Dangerous creature, so children go in pairs (9)

blocks.note: British name for a line of schoolchildren walking two by two

annotation.surface: A zoo trip warning: there is a crocodile about, so the pupils must hold hands.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a crocodile is a long line of schoolchildren walking in pairs, as on a school outing.
annotation.definitionFit: The crocodile is a large predatory reptile, dangerous to people.

entries.clue: Leader of communists executed and replaced (7)

indicatorNotes.Leader of: the leader is the front letter

annotation.surface: A purge: the communist leader is put to death and someone else installed.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a coup; 'and' only joins the wordplay to the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Something replaced has been changed for something else.

entries.clue: Satellite phones bosses each cut by half (6)

indicatorNotes.each cut by half: both words lose half their letters

annotation.surface: Office cutbacks: every manager's mobile allowance halved.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Satellite phones' reads as one phrase, but the satellite is the definition on its own. Phobos is a moon of Mars.
annotation.definitionFit: Phobos is the larger of the two moons of Mars, a natural satellite.

entries.clue: Just me on bank (6)

indicatorNotes.on: in a down clue, on means placed above

blocks.note: to bank on is to rely on

annotation.surface: A plea to depend on the speaker alone: just count on me.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bank' is not a riverside or a lender: to bank on someone is to rely on them.
annotation.definitionFit: Merely and just both mean only, as in 'just a scratch'.

entries.clue: Scorching temperatures destroy last piece of scrubland (4)

blocks.note: HEATH, scrubland, without its last letter H

annotation.surface: A heatwave that finishes off the last scraps of dry vegetation.
annotation.walkthrough: A heath is open land covered in heather and scrub, common in southern England.
annotation.definitionFit: Heat is the condition of high temperature, so scorching temperatures.

entries.clue: Swagger round Los Angeles with English Ballet (4,4)

indicatorNotes.round: the outer word goes round the inner

annotation.surface: A strutting tour of Los Angeles alongside the English Ballet company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'English Ballet' reads like the name of a company, but English gives only its abbreviation, added after the container is built.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake is perhaps the best-known ballet of all.

entries.clue: Silver, inferior but shiny (5)

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

annotation.surface: A verdict on cheap silverware: poor quality, but it gleams.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface pits silver's poor quality against its shine; AG is the chemical symbol.
annotation.definitionFit: Something aglow is glowing, bright and shining.

entries.clue: Elegant young bird losing tail (4)

indicatorNotes.losing tail: a word's tail is its end, so a word losing its tail drops its last letter

blocks.note: CHICK without its last letter K

annotation.surface: A stylish chick that has lost its tail feathers.
annotation.walkthrough: The tail of a word is its last letter, so CHICK drops the K.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: chic, borrowed from French, means stylish, which is elegant.

entries.clue: Prejudiced individual interrupted by quiet tycoon (3,4)

indicatorNotes.interrupted by: the second part breaks into the first

annotation.surface: A bigot being quietly shushed mid-rant by a business magnate.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes the tycoon the one doing the interrupting; he is the definition, and SH breaks into BIGOT.
annotation.definitionFit: A big shot is an important, powerful person, such as a tycoon.

entries.clue: Three lakes surrounding one European city (5)

indicatorNotes.surrounding: the outer letters surround the inner

annotation.surface: A European city ringed by three lakes around a single island, perhaps.
annotation.walkthrough: 'European city' reads as one phrase, but European supplies only E, and 'city' alone defines Lille, in northern France.
annotation.definitionFit: Lille is a large city in northern France.

entries.clue: Turf very dry at first (3)

annotation.surface: A lawn that began the summer bone dry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Very dry' looks like one phrase describing the turf; 'very' is SO on its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A sod is a piece of turf, grass with its roots and soil.

entries.clue: Transport vehicle by railway and A-road (5,4)

annotation.surface: A list of transport options: by car, by rail, or along a main road.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Transport' also means to thrill, as does carry away; and an A-road is a British main road, here split into A and road.
annotation.definitionFit: To transport is to carry away, either physically or in rapture.
